extracted.intended_audience: law students, patent attorneys, patent agents, and practitioners involved in patent prosecution and litigation
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and procedural rules governing actions after patent issuance (disclaimers, certificates of correction, reissue, reexamination, term extension) and related federal-court litigation matters (who may sue or be sued, jurisdiction, venue, presumption of validity, stays).

rubrics_metrics.name: Appeals from PTO decisions to courts
rubrics_metrics.description: If an applicant is dissatisfied with a Board of Patent Appeals and Interferences decision in an appeal from a final rejection, he or she may initiate a civil action against the Commissioner in the U.S. District Court for the District of Columbia (35 U.S.C. §§ 145, 146); or an applicant may appeal directly from the PTO to the Federal Circuit (35 U.S.C. § 141).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In the district court the question of the applicant’s right to a patent is tried de novo. Appeals from the district court go exclusively to the Federal Circuit; in practice most appeals are taken directly to the Federal Circuit. Federal Circuit decisions are subject to Supreme Court certiorari.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disclaimers and dedications by patent owner
rubrics_metrics.description: A patent owner may disclaim or dedicate to the public the entire patent term (all claims), the entire term of any complete claim, or the terminal part of the term of the entire patent (but not a terminal part of only some claims) (35 U.S.C. § 253).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A fee (set by regulation) is paid, the PTO publishes notice in the Official Gazette and prints copies for attachment to printed patents. Typical motivations: substantial question as to validity, duplicate coverage ('double patenting') requiring terminal disclaimer so patents expire same day (terminal disclaimer effective only for obviousness-type double patenting).

rubrics_metrics.name: Certificates of Correction (PTO and applicant)
rubrics_metrics.description: The PTO must issue, without charge, a certificate under seal correcting printing errors in a patent and attach it to printed copies (35 U.S.C. § 254). An applicant is entitled, on payment of a fee, to a Certificate of Correction for clerical or typographical errors that were the applicant’s responsibility if it is obvious the error was made in good faith (35 U.S.C. § 255).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A PTO-issued certificate and an applicant-issued certificate have the same effect as if the patent had been issued correctly. The PTO will also issue certificates correcting inventorship either by court order or by petition; the inventorship error must have been made in good faith (35 U.S.C. § 256).

rubrics_metrics.name: Reissue requirements under 35 U.S.C. § 251
rubrics_metrics.description: A patent may be reissued by the PTO upon surrender of the original patent if, through error without deceptive intention, it is deemed wholly or partly inoperative or invalid (35 U.S.C. § 251).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Common bases for reissue: (1) claims too narrow or too broad; (2) inaccuracies in disclosure; (3) incorrect naming of inventors; (4) failure to claim foreign priority correctly; (5) failure to refer properly to a copending application. The reissue oath/declaration must set forth the error(s). Reissue must claim the same general invention and may not add new matter or recapture surrendered subject matter. Claims may be broadened only if the reissue is filed within two years of issuance and signed by the inventor; after two years claims may only be narrowed (if not being broadened, assignee may sign). Reissue files are public; protests allowed; examiner may consider de novo all patentability issues. When reissued, cancellations are bracketed and additions italicized. Intervening rights may arise for parties who practiced subject matter not covered by original claims but covered by reissued claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Entry of citations of prior art into patent file (35 U.S.C. § 301)
rubrics_metrics.description: Any person may cite patents or printed publications for entry into the file of a patent during its enforceability to inform the PTO and the patent owner of prior art that may affect the patent; the submitter may remain anonymous (35 U.S.C. § 301).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A copy of each citation is to be served on the patent owner; absent evidence of service, the PTO notifies the owner. Such citations can form the basis for a request for reexamination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reexamination request standard and timing
rubrics_metrics.description: Any person may request reexamination (including the patent owner) by paying the required fee (35 U.S.C. § 302). The standard for granting reexamination is that a "substantial new question of patentability" is raised by the cited art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The decision on the request, based on that criterion, must be made within three months of filing. If the request is denied, it can be petitioned to the Commissioner within one month. Fee information (as of text): fee $2,250 (set high to discourage frivolous requests), and if reexamination is not granted $1,690 of the fee is refunded (37 C.F.R. §§ 1.20(c), 1.26(c)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Reexamination procedure and limits
rubrics_metrics.description: If reexamination is ordered, the patent owner may file within two months a Patent Owner's Statement showing why claims are patentable and present narrowing amendments; the requester (other than owner) may reply within two months (37 C.F.R. §§ 1.530, 1.535). After the statement period, reexamination proceeds ex parte similar to prosecution; appeals from final rejection are available. In reexamination, claims may only be narrowed, although new claims no broader than the original claims may be added.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: On completion, the PTO issues a Notice of Intent to Issue a Reexamination Certificate and then the Reexamination Certificate. The certificate will: (a) cancel unpatentable claims; (b) confirm patentable claims; (c) incorporate amended or new patentable claims; (d) make approved changes in the description; (e) include any statutory disclaimer filed; (f) refer to unamended claims held invalid on final holding by another forum on non-patent/printed-publication grounds; (g) refer to any claims not reexamined; (h) be mailed to patent owner and requester; (i) refer to dependent claims determined patentable. Reexamination files are public; any interested person may file citations during reexamination. Citations received after reexamination ordered are entered after completion and require a new request if further consideration is desired. Intervening rights can arise from reexamination (35 U.S.C. § 307(b)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Patent term extension under 35 U.S.C. § 156
rubrics_metrics.description: The term of a patent for a product, method of using a product, or method of manufacturing a product will be extended if the product was subject to a regulatory review period before commercial use and the extension is applied for during the unexpired patent term (35 U.S.C. § 156).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The length of the extension is generally equal to the regulatory review period, subject to exceptions. The primary purpose is to compensate for lengthy regulatory review (e.g., under the Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act) that consumes patent term and limits exploitation of the patent. Additionally, extensions under 35 U.S.C. § 154 (as amended by GATT-implementing legislation) can compensate up to five years for time lost due to interference proceedings, secrecy orders, or reversal of nonpatentability on appeal; calculation governed by statute.

rubrics_metrics.name: Who may assert the patent right (owners, assignees, licensees)
rubrics_metrics.description: A patent gives its owner the right to exclude others from making, using, offering for sale, selling, or importing the invention. This right can be shared or transferred by assignment or by license; many different parties may have sufficient interest to enforce a patent (35 U.S.C. § 261).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Three types of assignment: (1) convey all ownership interest (common); (2) convey a fractional undivided share (co-owner problems — absent agreement co-owners have equal rights despite unequal shares); (3) convey all interest for a determined time or place (grant—rare). Anyone with the entire ownership interest can enforce the patent alone. An assignee owning an undivided share generally must act in conjunction with co-owners. An exclusive licensee has rights approximating ownership but cannot usually assert the patent alone; typically must act with the patent owner, though the exclusive licensee can usually compel the owner to join as an involuntary plaintiff; a nonexclusive licensee cannot assert the patent right at all.

rubrics_metrics.name: Indispensable parties and co-owner enforcement
rubrics_metrics.description: Co-owners are usually indispensable parties to a suit to enforce a patent; the suit cannot proceed without all co-owners. Absent agreement, an unwilling co-owner cannot be compelled to join in enforcement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Problems arise when a co-owner attempts to proceed without others, when an exclusive licensee attempts to proceed without the patent owner/licensor, or when the patent owner attempts to proceed without an exclusive licensee. Courts have held exclusive licensees can often compel the owner to join; owners can often compel licensees to join.

rubrics_metrics.name: Who can attack a patent (declaratory judgment standing)
rubrics_metrics.description: A declaratory-judgment action that a patent is invalid, unenforceable, or not infringed can be brought by any party, including assignees and licensees, if two conditions are satisfied: (1) the patent owner acted to create in the prospective plaintiff a reasonable apprehension of being charged with infringement; and (2) the plaintiff has a sufficient interest at stake.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A sufficient interest exists if the plaintiff makes, uses, or sells an accused product, contributes to allegedly infringing activity, induces allegedly infringing activity, indemnifies alleged infringers, or has the intention and ability to engage in the allegedly infringing activity. The declaratory judgment must be brought against a proper defendant — generally one who alone could assert the patent right. Federal Circuit decisions articulate variations of the test but retain two core elements: defendant acts indicating intent to enforce patent, and plaintiff acts that might subject it or its customers to suit for infringement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Federal subject-matter jurisdiction in patent cases
rubrics_metrics.description: Federal courts have had exclusive subject-matter jurisdiction over patent-law cases since 1836 (28 U.S.C. § 1338(a)). Jurisdiction extends only when a well-pleaded complaint establishes that federal patent law creates the cause of action or the plaintiff's right necessarily depends on resolving a substantial question of federal patent law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The 'well-pleaded complaint' rule includes compulsory counterclaims for patent infringement. Many common disputes (e.g., breach of contract to pay royalties, removal of cloud on title) do not 'arise under' the patent laws and therefore may not fall within exclusive federal jurisdiction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Venue statutes applicable to patent cases
rubrics_metrics.description: Venue depends upon the cause of action: for patent infringement by a nonalien defendant 28 U.S.C. § 1400(b) (the patent venue statute) applies; for other patent-related causes of action the general venue statute 28 U.S.C. § 1391 applies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When multiple patents are asserted, each patent must be treated separately for venue purposes; venue must be appropriate for each asserted patent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patent venue statute §1400(b) tests
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 1400(b) provides two independent tests for venue: (1) where the defendant resides, and (2) where the defendant has committed acts of infringement and has a regular and established place of business.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the defendant is an individual, residence is domicile. If the defendant is a corporation, it resides in any judicial district in which it is subject to personal jurisdiction at the time the action is commenced (apply 28 U.S.C. § 1391(c) interpretation). The 1988 amendments to §1391(c) affected corporate venue and influenced §1400(b) application (see VE Holding).

rubrics_metrics.name: Acts that satisfy §1400(b) (what constitutes 'in the district')
rubrics_metrics.description: For venue the focus is on whether the act occurred in the district, not whether the act constitutes infringement. Acts satisfying §1400(b) include making, using, offering for sale, selling an accused product or process in the district; inducing another to make/use/sell in the district; and contributing in the district to another's making/using/selling.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: 'Making' means manufacturing or assembling; 'using' means actual use (not mere possession). 'Selling' has been historically ambiguous—some jurisdictions required a formal sale under the UCC, others required solicitation plus demonstrations; GATT-implementing legislation expanded acts (e.g., offer to sell) that may satisfy venue. For inducement/contributory claims, venue is appropriate only where the alleged inducer or contributor acted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regular and established place of business requirement for venue
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 1400(b)'s second test requires the defendant have a 'regular and established place of business' in the district as well as commit infringing acts there.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This element does not require the place of business be related to the alleged infringing act; inquiry focuses on whether the defendant does business through a permanent and continuous presence in the district. A 'place of business' need not be a fixed physical office or store.

rubrics_metrics.name: Application of the general venue statute §1391
rubrics_metrics.description: When the plaintiff alleges a cause of action involving a patent but not a patent-infringement action against a nonalien defendant (e.g., declaratory judgment actions), the general venue statute 28 U.S.C. § 1391 applies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even though a declaratory judgment action may be the 'mirror image' of an infringement action, a different venue statute applies; courts have treated these venue questions distinctly (see VE Holding).

rubrics_metrics.name: Presumption of validity and burden of proof to show invalidity
rubrics_metrics.description: A patent is presumed valid (35 U.S.C. § 282); each claim is presumed valid independently. The burden on a party challenging validity is to show, by clear and convincing evidence, that the patent is invalid.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts are not bound by the PTO's decision to issue a patent but give deference to the agency. If a challenger presents no evidence different from that reviewed by the examiner, the challenge is difficult. The challenger’s task is easier if material evidence not considered by the PTO is presented, but the legal burden of proof remains unchanged.

rubrics_metrics.name: Court stays of proceedings in patent cases
rubrics_metrics.description: A court has inherent power to stay proceedings before it to control its docket (Landis v. North American Co.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Whether to stay a particular case (or enjoin participation in another proceeding) involves usual docket-control considerations and sometimes patent-unique priorities. GATT-implementing legislation added 28 U.S.C. § 1659, which mandates a stay in certain circumstances involving a parallel infringement proceeding before the U.S. International Trade Commission.
